title: The grandfather's rug
hookLine: Abd al-Muttalib lets the boy sit on his rug by the Ka'ba, where no one else sat

lines: A RUG IN THE KA'BA'S SHADE.
A SMALL BOY SITS ON IT.
cards: In the shade of the Ka'ba, a rug is spread on the ground. It belongs to one man, Abd al-Muttalib, the old chief who found Zamzam again. His grown sons sit around its edge, the sirah says, and not one of them sits on it.
Then a small boy, an orphan who has just lost his mother, walks past the circle of men and sits down on it. Today: Abd al-Muttalib.

teach.h: THE UNCLES REACH TO MOVE HIM.
teach.b: The boy is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, newly back in Mecca without his mother. Ibn Ishaq tells this scene briefly. His uncles reach for him to pull him off, because the rug is their father's place, and nobody takes it.

Leave my son alone, he says, in the sirah's telling, and he speaks of a great future for the boy. Then he sits him beside him and strokes his back, pleased with whatever the boy does. That's the whole scene.
It's small, but it holds a lot. First, a seat. In a tribal town, where you sit says who you are.
The rug by the Ka'ba is honor, made visible. Second, a hand.
The uncles' hands reach to move him; the grandfather's hand rests on his back. Third, a word: my son. Not my grandson, not my dead son's boy.
The man who once vowed to sacrifice a son, and ransomed Abdullah with camels, now calls Abdullah's orphan his own. And fourth, a lesson the Prophet would later put into words.

teach.h: MERCY TO THE YOUNG, HONOR TO THE OLD.
teach.b: In a hadith collected by al-Tirmidhi, he says that whoever does not show mercy to the young, and honor to the old, is not one of us.
Both halves are on the rug that day: an old man honored by his sons, and a child given mercy by the old man. The sirah does not tell us what the boy felt. It only tells us where he sat.

how: Muslims teach kindness to children and respect for elders together, often citing the hadith that whoever does not show mercy to the young and honor the old is not one of us.

o: the chief's rug, the seat of honor in Mecca
the stone house at Mecca, walked around by pilgrims
the council hall where Quraysh's elders met

games.q: the grandfather's rug — tap the pairs.
p: mercy to the young, honor to the old

s: the grown sons sat on the rug with their father
they sat around it; no one sat on it, the sirah says.
Abd al-Muttalib called the boy my son
in the sirah he tells the uncles to leave his son alone.
the sirah describes what the boy was feeling
it tells us only where he sat, and the hand on his back.

games.q: you're Abd al-Muttalib. your grandson has walked onto the rug no one sits on, and your sons reach to move him. what do you do?
o: let them move him; a rule is a rule.
tell them to leave him, and sit him beside you.
get up and give him the whole rug.
games.why: in the sirah he says leave my son alone, sits him close, and strokes his back.

practice: Think of a child in your life, a son or daughter, a niece, a student, the kid next door, and of a rug they're usually kept off: a conversation, a table, a quiet hour that's yours.

Picture yourself moving over and patting the place beside you, and the child sitting down in it. If you pray, you can ask Allah for patience with the young; if not, just stay with that picture a moment.

wordCard.voice: Ka'ba. In its shade, the orphaned boy sat on his grandfather's rug, where none of the grown sons would sit. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a place beside the elder. Tomorrow, Abu Talib's house. Day seven hundred ten, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Abd al-Muttalib's rug in the shade of the Ka'ba; 'leave my son alone')
